articles.title: Brief Peppermint Odour Exposure and Immediate Free Recall of a Visual Object Array: A Three-Arm Randomised Experiment
articles.content: Background: Odours reach limbic and prefrontal targets through a uniquely direct pathway and are often claimed to enhance cognition, yet experimental evidence for specific essential oils is mixed and frequently confounded by expectancy. We tested whether a brief inhalation of peppermint or clove essential oil, compared with no odour, alters immediate free recall of a visual object array. Methods: Sixty healthy adults aged 18-50 years were randomly allocated to peppermint oil, clove oil or no odour (n = 20 each). After 30 s of inhalation (or none), participants studied a 4 x 4 array of 16 pictured items for 20 s and then wrote down every item they could recall, without time limit. Groups were compared with one-way and Welch ANOVA, Welch-corrected pairwise tests with Holm correction, Hedges' g with 95% confidence intervals and Bayes factors. Results: Recall differed across conditions (Welch F(2, 37.0) = 8.53, p < .001; omega2 = 0.14). Participants exposed to peppermint recalled more items (11.20 +/- 2.14) than those exposed to no odour (8.45 +/- 2.04; g = 1.29, 95% CI [0.61, 1.97], p(Holm) < .001, BF10 = 134). Clove (9.55 +/- 3.19) did not differ reliably from either no odour (g = 0.40, p(Holm) = .203) or peppermint (g = 0.60, p(Holm) = .127; BF10 = 1.29). Conclusions: A single brief exposure to peppermint oil was associated with substantially better immediate recall than no odour. Because the peppermint-clove contrast was inconclusive and no placebo odour was used, the data do not establish an odour-specific effect; general arousal and expectancy remain plausible contributors. Pre-registered, laboratory-based replications with placebo odours, blinding and arousal measures are required.
articles.author: Akar, B., Altıntas, T.

articles.title: Myelin Governs Hippocampal Network Function through the Extracellular Space it Occupies, Not Only the Axons it Insulates
articles.content: Myelin, the multilamellar sheath wrapping neuronal axons, enables saltatory conduction. Beyond electrical insulation, myelin occupies volume, and therefore shapes the extracellular space (ECS) through which interstitial fluid flows and neurotransmitter diffuses. How these two roles interact is unknown. We built a multi-scale model of hippocampal CA1 coupling lattice Boltzmann simulations of ECS flow to detailed networks of reconstructed neurons and glia. Demyelination enlarged the ECS volume fraction from 28 to 43 per cent up to 43 to 70 per cent across layers, lowered tortuosity from about 1.7 to 1.4, raised effective diffusivity from 0.35 to 0.50 of free solution and shortened solute breakthrough times by roughly a third, while raising flow speed yet lowering viscous dissipation. Because transmitter concentration scales inversely with that volume, synaptic driving force fell: postsynaptic potential amplitude declined with wrap count and transmission failed entirely below four of sixteen wraps. In 200-cell networks, demyelination halved firing (pyramidal 7.9 to 4.4 Hz), rendered discharge burst-dominated, reduced band power by up to 8.7-fold and displaced the population state, which a classifier separated at 100 per cent accuracy, whereas an inflammatory glial census left every functional measure unchanged. Driving myelin continuously from intact to 12.5 per cent and back recovered the same threshold near four wraps, and firing rate and spectral power returned fully to baseline. Myelin thus governs circuit function through the space it vacates as well as the axons it insulates, with opposite consequences for clearance and for signalling, a dissociation that may matter in demyelinating disease.
articles.author: Jia, X., Zeng, C., Liu, L., Gao, T., Bi, J., Zeng, Z., Liang, L., Qi, C., Lin, F., Cheng, F.

articles.title: Path knockout: an analysis tool for connectome-driven circuit discovery
articles.content: Neural circuits in the brain transform sensory information into perceptual, emotional and motor output. The connectome -- a synaptic-resolution wiring diagram of all neurons in a nervous system -- provides a neuroanatomical blueprint for identifying different circuits that mediate specific computations. However, its sheer scale and complexity pose a significant challenge in extracting functionally relevant multi-synaptic pathways. Here we established path knockout, a connectome analysis method that identifies dominant multi-synaptic pathways. Path knockout uses the input fraction of each synaptic connection as a surrogate for the probability that information transfer succeeds across that synapse and calculates approximate probability, or connection strength, that at least one path succeeds among all multi-synaptic paths between defined source and sink neuron populations. It then quantifies the importance of each interneuron by assessing the impact of its removal on the connection strength. We demonstrate that path knockout outperforms other methods for pathway analysis and identifies known and novel interneurons in the Drosophila circuits. Using path knockout, we identified a convergent circuit motif linking sexually dimorphic aggression command neurons to a shared isomorphic visual pursuit pathway. Path knockout is implemented such that it runs in minutes on a standard computer. Thus, path knockout provides a scalable and generalizable framework for connectome-driven circuit discovery.
articles.author: McGrath, R., Hattori, D.

articles.title: A medial entorhinal connectome reveals compartmentalized microcircuit architecture
articles.content: The medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) transforms multimodal inputs into spatial representations, but the synaptic architecture underlying its computations remains unclear. Here we generated a synapse-resolution connectomic dataset spanning all six layers of mouse MEC and the adjacent parasubiculum with serial electron microscopy, providing a continuous volume for mapping cellular organization and connectivity across layers and regions. We found that clustered pyramidal neurons in MEC layer II extended oblique apical dendrites with a dorsolateral bias and long-range myelinated axons within the layer. Exhaustive reconstruction of one cluster revealed a central exclusion core (ExC) that spatially partitioned basal dendritic architecture and synaptic connectivity. A spatially constrained growth model reproduced the position-dependent dendritic patterns. Within the ExC, pyramidal neurons formed a compact recurrent excitatory network and converged onto shared inhibitory partners. Basket cells (BC) and recurrent Martinotti cells provided perisomatic and apical-dendritic feedback, respectively. Dense, compact reciprocal connectivity between L2P neurons and BCs within the ExC, together with BC axonal bands extending beyond the ExC, suggests a potential circuit mechanism for generating temporally structured inhibitory output from the pyramidal-cell cluster along directionally extended axons. Together, these findings link cellular-scale geometry and synaptic wiring to emergent circuit dynamics that extend from dense computation within individual clusters to region-wide modulation, providing a connectomic foundation for understanding the circuit basis of spatial navigation.
articles.author: Shi, T., Chen, Y., Jin, H., Jiang, H., Chen, X., Xiong, Z., Wu, F., Zhang, R.

articles.title: Wolffia globosa -derived nanovesicles as a natural source of bioactive metabolites with neuroprotective potential against methylglyoxal-induced oxidative stress
articles.content: Plant-derived nanovesicles (PDNVs) have attracted increasing attention for their potential biomedical applications, particularly in oxidative stress-related diseases and neuroprotection. Wolffia globosa, an emerging functional food and potential future food source, is rich in phytochemicals associated with health-promoting properties. Harnessing W. globosa-derived nanovesicles (WGNVs) represents a promising strategy for expanding the biomedical applications of this plant. In this study, WGNVs were isolated and characterized, and their neuroprotective potential was evaluated in vitro. The isolated WGNVs exhibited nanoscale dimensions and a lipid bilayer structure. Biochemical analyses revealed substantial total phenolic and flavonoid contents, alongside intrinsic antioxidant activities. Untargeted metabolomic profiling identified a diverse repertoire of metabolites, including major constituents subsequently validated using independent analytical approaches. These findings provided a foundation for investigating the neuroprotective effects of WGNVs in a methylglyoxal (MGX)-induced model of neuronal oxidative stress. High-resolution confocal microscopy demonstrated the cellular localization of WGNVs within neuronal cells, providing evidence of interactions between plant-derived nanovesicles and neuronal cells. WGNV treatment attenuated MGX-induced free radical accumulation and oxidative stress responses while preserving cellular morphology integrity. Collectively, this study provides foundational evidence of the physicochemical characteristics, metabolite composition, and in vitro neuroprotective potential of WGNVs. These findings highlight WGNVs as a promising naturally derived nanocarrier platform for investigating plant-animal interkingdom interactions and exploring potential therapeutic applications across a broad range of biomedical fields.
articles.author: Khongkla, E., Boonsnongcheep, P., Srisaisup, M., Charuraksa, T.

articles.title: Dissociable norepinephrine and dopamine representations during strategic decision-making and reward learning
articles.content: Adaptive decision-making in competitive environments requires learning from immediate reward outcomes while tracking longer-timescale information to adjust behavioural strategies and remain unpredictable against others. Dopamine (DA) and norepinephrine (NE) have long been implicated in reward-guided behaviours, but their contributions to strategic choice remain unclear. We trained mice to play a zero-sum matching pennies game against a computer opponent that exploited regularities in their choice and reward history, such that optimal performance required stochastic choice decoupled from immediate reward. We combined fibre photometry recordings, behavioural and neural modelling, and a within-subject multi-task design to determine how NE and DA contribute to strategic choice in the matching pennies game versus reward-guided behaviour in a two-armed bandit (2AB) task. DA responses were dominated by trial-by-trial reward outcomes and consistently tracked model-derived reward prediction errors (RPE) across tasks and behavioural states. In contrast, NE activity reflected salient task events, predicted upcoming choice switches, and tracked longer-timescale variables including model-inferred behavioural strategy and average reward rate. In addition, NE responses were selectively enhanced following rewarded switches when these outcomes were informative for deciding whether to stay in or switch from the current strategy; and this enhancement could not be explained by RPE. Incorporating pre-choice NE activity into a reinforcement-learning model to modulate choice generation improved model prediction in matching pennies but not in the 2AB task. Together, these findings reveal complementary neuromodulatory correlates of competitive decision-making across timescales: DA primarily guides learning from immediate outcomes through RPE, whereas NE additionally represents contextual information and choice stochasticity relevant for shaping long-term strategies.
articles.author: Aloor, J., Sit, T. P., Geuter, J., Tutt, J. O., Duan, C. A.

articles.title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNS for Flexible Working Memory
articles.content: Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in neural systems and has been implicated in cognitive functions such as memory and sequence processing. However, its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear. Here, we studied OPC by training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, we found that OPC emerges in the RNN spontaneously: the memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with oscillation amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablation studies identified three key elements required for OPC: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis revealed the emergence of content and time cells in the trained RNN, and they process item identity and sequence order separately. Recurrent connectivity analysis revealed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups. Inspired by these findings, we proposed a neural circuit model which reproduces OPC through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. Together, this study reveals how OPC arises from network structures and task demands, offers insights into the implementation and computational mechanisms of OPC in biological systems, and inspires us to develop computational models for human-like cognitive functions.
articles.author: Lu, K., Chu, T., TUERHONG, A., Sun, Y., Luo, H., Fang, F., WU, S.

articles.title: Multi-scale place fields provide a predictive basis for hierarchical control
articles.content: Hippocampal place cells typically exhibit unimodal spatial selectivity in small enclosures, but express multiple, irregularly spaced fields in environments of naturalistic scale. However, existing predictive-map theories of the hippocampus do not scale well to large environments and do not account for these heterogeneous place field characteristics. Here, we introduce the factorised hierarchical successor representation (fHSR), a predictive map that supports hierarchical control using subgoal-directed subroutines. We show that the fHSR allows efficient generalisation across tasks, scaling favourably with environmental size, and it reproduces key statistical and topological characteristics of multi-scale CA1 place cell activity in rats and bats. Analyses of experimental data further confirmed a novel prediction of the fHSR: population firing rates exhibit spatial periodicity with a characteristic wavelength independent of environmental size. These results identify the integration of hierarchical control and predictive representations as a normative principle that unifies efficient navigation with the spatial organisation of hippocampal activity.
articles.author: Yu, C., Maimon, S. R., Rich, P. D., Eliav, T., Las, L., Lee, A. K., Ulanovsky, N., Lengyel, M.

articles.title: BundleMorphometry: Spatially Resolved White Matter Bundle Shape Analysis Using Nonlinear Streamline-based Registration
articles.content: Diffusion MRI tractometry quantifies microstructural properties along white matter (WM) bundles but does not directly measure their geometry, potentially overlooking localized morphological alterations. Here, we introduce BundleMorphometry, a framework for quantifying local WM bundle shape using the analytical Jacobian of nonlinear streamline-based registration. Individual subject bundles are registered to a reference atlas bundle using BundleWarp, a streamline-based nonlinear registration method. We derive the analytical Jacobian of the resulting deformation field and compute its log-determinant (log det J) to quantify local expansion and compression at each streamline point. To enable spatially resolved group comparisons, these measurements are projected onto the two-dimensional grid, capturing variations along and across each bundle. We evaluated BundleMorphometry using two clinical datasets comprising patients with glioma and Parkinson's disease (PD). In the glioma dataset, BundleMorphometry revealed spatially extensive deformation patterns in lesion-affected WM bundles that were not captured by displacement magnitude alone. Additionally, in a group analysis of the PD dataset (32 patients and 32 healthy controls), we identified significant localized morphological differences in the corpus callosum forceps major, mid-body and right spinothalamic tract, with distinct patterns of expansion and compression. These findings demonstrate the potential of BundleMorphometry to advance conventional tractometry by enabling spatially resolved analysis of bundle morphology.
articles.author: Dasanayake, D., Amit, S. N., Chandio, B. Q.

articles.title: Circuit regulation along an activity continuum shapes flexible and stable representations during learning
articles.content: Learning requires neural representations to flexibly incorporate new information while progressively stabilizing to support enduring memories. How neural circuits balance these demands remains unclear. Here, we identify complementary mechanisms supporting representational flexibility and stability in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), a key component of the cognitive map for memory-guided navigation. Longitudinal calcium imaging in mice learning novel virtual environments revealed a persistent axis of excitatory neuronal activity associated with distinct representational dynamics. Low-activity neurons exhibited intermittent activation that varied with learning stages and greater learning-dependent representational refinement, flexibly shifting their encoding from landmarks toward reward locations. By contrast, high-activity neurons exhibited more persistent activation and maintained more stable spatial representations. Dopaminergic pre-reward ramping was associated with the emergence of reward encoding in low-activity neurons, whereas interactions with inhibitory interneurons contributed to the stability of high-activity neurons. Notably, interneurons exhibited activity changes opposing those of excitatory neurons during learning, and their transient activation upon novelty exposure delayed excitatory representational remodeling, stabilization, and behavioral learning, suggesting that inhibitory circuits gate learning-dependent representational dynamics. Together, these findings reveal how activity-dependent excitatory neuronal organization and circuit-level regulation enable complementary forms of representational flexibility and stability to coexist, facilitating the incorporation of novel experiences into stable, context-specific cognitive maps that support learning.
